name: Wimbum (Limbum)
place: Palace of the Fon of Mbot, Ndu-Nkambe (Donga-Mantung, North-West)
overview: In the majority on the Nkambe plateau, the Wimbum arrived there from the Tikar region, in search of fertile land and to escape Fulani raids. The sacred kingship of the fon, powerful secret societies, weaving, palm wine and maize beer characterise a culture close to those of the North-West and the West.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group living in harmony with the Mbororo and the neighbouring villages (Nwa, Ako, Misaje, Banso).
Limbum dominates, but many also speak Fulfulde and Hausa; it is not spoken elsewhere.
Mixed group: mixed marriages are accepted, even though parents prefer marriage within the group.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The Nkambe plateau is the land of the ancestors.
Having come from the Tikar country (Adamawa) via Kimi, the Wimbum were looking for water and fertile land and fleeing Fulani raids; they have kept no ties with their point of departure.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Royal society: decisions are made at the chiefdom, by consensus between the fon and his close collaborators.
A member of clan A can inherit or be enthroned in clan B, and vice versa.
Unmarried people do not speak in public; relations with the in-laws are cordial.
The young bride (ŋgwāaŋgù) looks at neither her father-in-law nor her husband; one bends before the fon without looking at him, and only initiated men greet him by clapping three times.
You do not shake hands with the notables, the fon or the queen mother.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman always joins her husband's home.
Ages given: 20 for the man, 18 for the woman; according to some, circumcision at about 18 makes the boy a man.
Steps: engagement (the boy offers a ring), inquiry and acceptance, courtship (services rendered to the girl's family), presentation and bride price, accompanying the wife to her husband's home.

Bride price: a goat (oath not to give the girl to another), the njàp, clothes for the fon, a wrapper for the queen mother (sign of maturity), blankets; formerly cowries, bracelets and hoes, then money.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The ancestor cult takes place at sowing (March), at harvest (August), at the death and at the enthronement of a fon.
Sacred places: Ndáp ŋgɔ̀ŋg and Ngù ŋgɔ̀ŋg at the palace, the lɛ̀'kòŋg at the heart of the family house, the ŋkōo maala' (the sub-chief's quarter), the tùnyù and tùndzìsiŋ hills, the rivers.
A birth can mark the return of a fon, a queen mother, an ancestor or a departed twin; death leads back to the ancestors, who speak through dreams and divination.

Taboos: the fon never sees or touches a corpse; women must not see the ŋwāròŋ, the highest secret society; incest leads to exile or isolation until purification; on certain days, access to ritual sites is forbidden.
Theft is judged by the customary court and punished by the ŋwāròŋ.
Divination by the spider (ŋgāa), with wild fruits (kàkár), water, barks, ashes, feathers.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: weaving, palm wine harvesting, pottery, bamboo work. Women: farming, trade, knitting, embroidery.
The fon owns the land and delegates its management to the neighbourhood chiefs (fǎy), who may allocate plots to unmarried women.
Ancestral basketry intended for sale: baskets (kwàrákwārá, sòo, ŋkɛ̀ŋ), bags, chairs, trays.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Formerly, tɛ́' for men and njìkìtás for women; today, tòmákùr (“atiogho” or Bamenda outfit), ndop, and a two-piece wrapper with a blouse for women.
Traditional medicine, inherited from the ancestors, is considered effective and protective.
Beauty: a preserved natural complexion; for women, good conduct also counts.
Courtship: gifts, good conduct, talent as a singer or dancer.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Dances and rhythms: mfú' (dance of the mfú' men), ndzàŋ, sàambā, tàrá, kì∫ɛ́', mbàjà, ndзù', ndɔ́ŋ, mnsūu, tɔ̀'.
Instruments: ntʃùu, kìŋsūu horn, kwàkwàr, ŋgɛ̀m.
People dance at cultural festivals, funerals and enthronements; there is no festival common to all, but regional gatherings.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Food, clothing, architecture and traditional government bring the Wimbum closer to the peoples of the West and North-West.

sections.title: The names
items: There are names for girls, boys and twins, with no particular marker.
The name is given three to seven days after birth, at a ceremony; it does not change, but title-holders enrich it.
After a birth, the parents are called māa (mother) and bǎltá (father) rather than by their names.
The founder, Fon Mbòmnsa', is “the one who interrupts and settles problems”.

lessons.title: Who are the Wimbum (Limbum)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Wimbum (Limbum) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Wimbum (Limbum) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Wimbum (Limbum) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Wimbum (Limbum) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Wimbum (Limbum) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Wimbum (Limbum) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group living in harmony with the Mbororo and the neighbouring villages (Nwa, Ako, Misaje, Banso). • Limbum dominates, but many also speak fulfulde and Haoussa; it is not spoken elsewhere. • Mixed group: mixed marriages are accepted, even though parents prefer marriage within the group. • The Nkambe plateau is the land of the ancestors. • Having come from the Tikar country (Adamawa) through Kimi, the Wimbum were looking for water and fertile land and were fleeing Fulani raids; they have kept no ties with their point of departure.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority on the Nkambe plateau, the Wimbum arrived there from the Tikar region, in search of fertile land and to escape Fulani raids. The sacred kingship of the fon, powerful secret societies, weaving, palm wine and maize beer characterise a culture close to those of the North-West and the West.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Wimbum (Limbum) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Wimbum (Limbum)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Wimbum (Limbum) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Wimbum (Limbum) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Wimbum (Limbum) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Wimbum (Limbum) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Royal society: decisions are made at the chiefdom, by consensus between the fon and his close collaborators. • A member of clan A can inherit or be enthroned in clan B, and vice versa. • Unmarried people do not speak in public; relations with the in-laws are cordial. • The young bride (ŋgwāaŋgù) looks neither at her father-in-law nor at her husband; one bows before the fon without looking at him, and only initiated men greet him by clapping their hands three times. • One does not shake hands with notables, the fon or the queen mother.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Royal society: decisions are made at the chiefdom, by consensus between the fon and his close collaborators. A member of clan A can inherit or be enthroned in clan B, and vice versa. Unmarried people do not speak in public; relations with the in-laws are cordial.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Wimbum (Limbum), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Wimbum (Limbum)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Wimbum (Limbum), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Wimbum (Limbum).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Wimbum (Limbum), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Wimbum (Limbum).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: maize fufu and greens (bāa kwâa ba njàp), ŋkwǐ, garden egg (nyá'), pounded macabo (ntʃwá). • Drinks: maize beer (shàa), palm wine (mrù' bú). • Men: weaving, palm wine tapping, pottery, bamboo work. Women: farming, trade, knitting, embroidery.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Wimbum (Limbum) eat mainly bāa kwâa ba njàp, ŋkwǐ, nyá', ntʃwá. Traditional drinks: shàa, mrù' bú. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Wimbum (Limbum): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Wimbum (Limbum)
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Wimbum (Limbum), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Wimbum (Limbum) dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Wimbum (Limbum), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Wimbum (Limbum) dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Dances and rhythms: mfú' (dance of the mfú' men), ndzàŋ, sàambā, tàrá, kì∫ɛ́', mbàjà, ndзù', ndɔ́ŋ, mnsūu, tɔ̀'. • Instruments: ntʃùu, kìŋsūu horn, kwàkwàr, ŋgɛ̀m. • People dance at cultural festivals, funerals and enthronements; there is no festival common to all, but there are regional gatherings.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Wimbum (Limbum), traditional dances (mfú', sàambā, ndzàŋ) accompany the major moments of life: festivals, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: kìŋsūu, ntʃùu, kwàkwàr, ŋgɛ̀m. Festival(s): enthronement of the fon, regional cultural gatherings.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Wimbum (Limbum) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Wimbum (Limbum)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Wimbum (Limbum), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Wimbum (Limbum). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Wimbum (Limbum), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Wimbum (Limbum). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: weaving, palm wine harvesting, pottery, bamboo work. Women: farming, trade, knitting, embroidery. • The fon owns the land and delegates its management to the quarter heads (fǎy), who may allocate plots to unmarried women. • Ancestral basketry made for sale: baskets (kwàrákwārá, sòo, ŋkɛ̀ŋ), bags, chairs, trays.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: weaving, palm wine harvesting, pottery, bamboo work. Women: farming, trade, knitting, embroidery. The fon owns the land and delegates its management to the quarter heads (fǎy), who may allocate plots to unmarried women.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Wimbum (Limbum)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Wimbum (Limbum)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Wimbum (Limbum), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Wimbum (Limbum). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Wimbum (Limbum), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Wimbum (Limbum). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Ancestor worship takes place at sowing (March), at harvest (August), at the death and the enthronement of a fon. • Sacred places: Ndáp ŋgɔ̀ŋg and Ngù ŋgɔ̀ŋg at the palace, the lɛ̀'kòŋg at the heart of the family house, the ŋkōo maala' (the sub-chief's quarter), the hills tùnyù and tùndzìsiŋ, the rivers. • A birth may mark the return of a fon, a queen mother, an ancestor or a deceased twin; death leads back to the ancestors, who speak through dreams and divination. • Taboos: the fon never sees or touches a corpse; women must not see the ŋwāròŋ, the highest secret society; incest leads to exile or isolation until purification; on certain days, access to ritual sites is forbidden. • Theft is judged by the customary court and punished by the ŋwāròŋ.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The ancestor cult takes place at sowing (March), at harvest (August), at the death and at the enthronement of a fon. Sacred places: Ndáp ŋgɔ̀ŋg and Ngù ŋgɔ̀ŋg at the palace, the lɛ̀'kòŋg at the heart of the family house, the ŋkōo maala' (the sub-chief's neighbourhood), the hills tùnyù and tùndzìsiŋ, the rivers.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Wimbum (Limbum) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Wimbum (Limbum) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Limbum
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Wimbum (Limbum) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Wimbum (Limbum) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Wimbum (Limbum) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Wimbum (Limbum) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Limbum. • Greeting formulae: Mɛ̀ t∫a’ = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Í rāa wɛ̀ á? = morning greeting (one person); Í rāa wɛ̀ á? = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Mò’sír, Baa, Tár, kyè, Tâ. • The founder, Fon Mbòmnsa', is “the one who interrupts and settles problems”. • Food, clothing, architecture and traditional government bring the Wimbum close to the peoples of the West and North-West.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Limbum are the first steps towards communicating with the Wimbum (Limbum). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
